Here are verse-by-verse notes on Leviticus 2, drawn from the sources I was able to search and fetch.

---

## Leviticus 2: The Grain Offering — Verse-by-Verse Notes

### Overview

The Hebrew word for this offering is *minchah*, which fundamentally means "a gift" or "tribute" from an inferior to a superior. In Genesis 4:3–5 it describes both Cain's and Abel's offerings. Over time it became restricted to bloodless, vegetable offerings. Older translations (KJV) call it the "meat offering," but "meat" in 17th-century English meant "food" in general, not animal flesh. Modern translations render it "grain offering," "meal offering," or "cereal offering."

The grain offering was a "sweet aroma" (voluntary) offering, expressing thanksgiving, homage, and dedication. It normally accompanied the burnt offering and sometimes the peace offering (Numbers 15:1–10). It was the only Levitical blood sacrifice that was bloodless — no atonement for sin was accomplished by it. It recognised God's sovereignty and provision.

**Sources:** Precept Austin (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_2_commentary); Pulpit Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/); Ellicott (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html).

---

### v. 1 — "When anyone brings a grain offering to the LORD, his offering must consist of fine flour. He is to pour olive oil on it, put frankincense on it…"

**Fine flour.** Matthew Poole explains it was "searched, or sifted, and purged from all bran, it being fit that the best things should be offered to the best Being" (Enduring Word, citing Poole). Ellicott notes the flour was of wheat (Exodus 29:2), double the value of ordinary barley flour, and formed part of the Temple stores (1 Chronicles 9:29; 23:29) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

**Oil.** Olive oil functioned in Israelite cooking as butter does in Western cuisine (Ellicott). Symbolically, many commentators — particularly in charismatic/Pentecostal and Reformed traditions — see oil as representing the Holy Spirit. Enduring Word states: "It was also symbolic of the fact that our service, our offering, should be always in the presence and under the influence of the Holy Spirit" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/. Poole likewise notes that oil "may note the graces of the Holy Ghost, which are compared to oil, and anointing with it" (Poole on biblehub.com — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/leviticus/2.htm).

**Frankincense.** A costly imported spice from the south-eastern Arabian peninsula, used only in ritual ceremonies (Enduring Word, citing Peter-Contesse). Ellicott gives a very practical explanation: "The frankincense was designed to counteract the offensive smell arising from the quantity of the flesh burnt there, as is evident from the following verse, where it is stated that it is wholly to be burnt" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html. Poole, meanwhile, sees frankincense as typifying "Christ's satisfaction and intercession, which is compared to a sweet odour (Ephesians 5:2), and to incense (Revelation 8:3)" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/poole/leviticus/2.htm.

**"Anyone"** — Precept Austin notes the Hebrew word here is *nepesh* ("soul"), unlike *adam* in Leviticus 1:2, indicating any person, male or female, could bring this offering (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_2_commentary).

---

### v. 2 — "…bring it to Aaron's sons the priests. The priest shall take a handful of the flour and oil, together with all the frankincense, and burn this as a memorial portion on the altar…"

**The priest's role.** The offerer prepared the offering at home and brought it to the priests; from that point the priest officiated — taking the handful, burning the memorial portion (https://www.preceptaustin.org/leviticus_2_commentary).

**"Memorial" (*azkarah*).** Ellicott explains it was so called "because it was designed to bring the worshipper into the grateful remembrance of God, and to remind him, as it were, of His promise to accept the service of His people." He cites Psalm 20:4 and Acts 10:4 (Cornelius) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html. The Pulpit Commentary likewise notes it "acted as a memorial before God … being something which should cause God to think graciously of the offerer" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html. Constable adds the important nuance that the verb behind "memorial" "often carries the nuance of beginning to act on the basis of what is remembered" — prompting both the worshiper to live covenantally and the LORD to bless — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-2.html.

**All the frankincense** was burned — none was kept by the priests and none was mixed into the flour. It was placed on top (*put* frankincense on it, v. 1) and wholly consumed.

**"A pleasing aroma to the LORD."** This is the language of a "sweet savour" offering — voluntary, expressing worship rather than atoning for sin (Enduring Word — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/). It is accepted by God as an expression of thanksgiving.

---

### v. 3 — "The remainder … shall belong to Aaron and his sons; it is a most holy part of the offerings made by fire to the LORD."

**Provision for the priests.** The remainder — around a gallon (one omer) or more of flour — went to feed the priests and their families. The grain offering "apparently provided the main source of income for the priesthood" (Enduring Word, citing Rooker) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/. Ellicott notes the priests divided it among themselves and consumed it in the court of the sanctuary — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

**"Most holy" (*qodesh qodashim*).** Ellicott explains the Israelite offerings fell into two classes: *less holy* (thank offerings, firstborn, firstfruits, Passover — eatable in any clean place within the holy city by priests and their families) and *most holy* (incense, shewbread, sin and trespass offerings, and grain offerings — eatable only in the sanctuary court, by priests alone). The grain offering belonged to the "most holy" class — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

Enduring Word comments: "That it was called *most holy* of the offerings shows the high regard God has of our thankfulness" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

---

### vv. 4–7 — Three Methods of Preparation

**Three cooking methods** are specified: (1) baked in an oven (v. 4), (2) prepared on a flat griddle/plate (v. 5), and (3) cooked in a pan (v. 7, literally a deeper stew-pan or pot for boiling in oil).

**The oven** (v. 4). Ellicott describes it as "the portable pot, open at the top, about three feet high … still used in the East." Dough was thrown against the heated sides and baked in minutes — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

**The griddle/pan** (v. 5). Ellicott identifies this as "the iron fire-plate (Ezekiel 5:3), with a convex surface, which is placed horizontally upon stones about nine inches from the ground." Large thin cakes were laid on the convex surface and baked quickly — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

**The covered pan** (v. 7). A deeper vessel, corresponding more to a stew-pan or pot; cakes were boiled in oil. Enduring Word (citing Harrison and Harris) notes: "Authorities suggest that the cereal offering cooked in the [covered pan] would look rather like a modern deep-fried doughnut" or dumpling — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

**"Crumble it and pour oil on it"** (v. 6). The griddle-baked cake was not offered whole but broken in pieces and mixed/moistened with oil. Ellicott remarks that "bread, broken in pieces and steeped in oil, butter, milk, or sweet juices, still constitutes a favourite dish among the Bedouin Arabs" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html. Enduring Word notes the offering was prepared *at home* — the devotion to God began in the domestic sphere before being brought publicly to the Tabernacle — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

**All forms unleavened** — see notes on v. 11 below.

---

### vv. 8–10 — Presentation and Memorial Burning (Reprise)

These verses repeat and expand the procedure of vv. 2–3. The offerer brings the prepared offering to the priest, who brings it to the altar, removes the memorial portion, and burns it. The remainder belongs to the priests. Ellicott notes that during the Second Temple period, the pieces were put into a ministering vessel, oil and frankincense were added, and the vessel was carried to the altar — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

Enduring Word notes: "No matter what form it was in, the grain offering had to be prepared at home … This expression of devotion to God began at home and if offered with the right heart, was a sweet aroma to the LORD" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

---

### v. 11 — "No grain offering … may be made with leaven, for you are not to burn any leaven or honey as an offering made by fire to the LORD."

**Leaven (yeast).** Almost universally interpreted by traditional commentators as symbolising sin and corruption. Enduring Word explains that ancient Israelites brought leaven into dough through a pinch left over from the previous batch (like sourdough), and that "a little pinch of dough from the old batch made a whole new lump of dough rise and puff up, spreading through the entire new batch. Therefore, the work of leaven was considered an illustration of the work of sin and pride." This links to Jesus' warnings about "the leaven of the Pharisees" (hypocrisy), the Sadducees (rationalism), and Herod (worldliness) — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

The **Reformed** view (Ligonier) states: "No leaven or honey could be added … probably because decomposition occurs in the leavening process and therefore makes the grain evidence of the decay of sin" — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/grain-offering.

The **Catholic** reading (Haydock, following Challoner): "No leaven or honey was to be used in the sacrifice offered to God: to signify that we are to exclude from the pure worship of the gospel, all double-dealing and affection to carnal pleasures" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-2.html.

The Pulpit Commentary offers a distinctive practical explanation: leaven and honey were forbidden on the altar "owing, no doubt, to the effect of fire upon them in making them swell and froth, thus creating a repulsive appearance which … represents moral evil" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html.

JFB (Jamieson-Fausset-Brown) notes: "In the warm climates of the East leavened bread soon spoils, and hence it was regarded as the emblem of hypocrisy or corruption. Some, however, think that the prohibition was that leaven and honey were used in the idolatrous rites of the heathen" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/leviticus/2.htm.

**Honey.** Several explanations are offered:
- Enduring Word: honey was "a favourite thing to sacrifice to pagan deities. God did not want to be worshipped in the same way that false, pagan gods were worshipped" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.
- Poole: "To teach us that God's worship is not to be governed by men's fancies and appetites, to which honey might have been grateful, but by God's will" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/ (citing Poole).
- Ellicott: honey was used to produce fermentation, so it is excluded like leaven — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.
- Haydock (Catholic): honey was "incompatible with the other ingredients, to admonish us to lead a penitential life, and to keep at a greater distance from the customs of the pagans, who generally accompanied their oblations with honey" (citing Herodotus on Egyptian practice) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-2.html.

Enduring Word offers a memorable devotional observation: "Leaven can make things artificially sour and honey can make things artificially sweet. God did not want either of these in sacrifice. When we offer ourselves as a living sacrifice (Romans 12:1–2) He wants us to come just as we are, without artificially making ourselves more sour or sweet" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

---

### v. 12 — "You may bring them to the LORD as an offering of firstfruits, but they are not to be offered on the altar as a pleasing aroma."

The Pulpit Commentary insists that the paragraph break before v. 12 in older translations is misleading. The sense is: leaven and honey *may* be brought as an oblation of firstfruits, but they must not be burned on the altar. They are offered to the LORD (and presumably go to the priests), but not via the altar fire — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html.

Ellicott agrees: "This verse mentions an exception to the rule … leaven and honey, which are excluded from the meat offerings, may be used with firstfruits. Hence they are mentioned with firstfruits (Leviticus 23:17; 2 Chronicles 31:5)" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html. The classic example is the two wave-loaves at Pentecost (Leviticus 23:17), which were leavened.

---

### v. 13 — "And you shall season each of your grain offerings with salt. You must not leave the salt of the covenant of your God out of your grain offering; you are to add salt to each of your offerings."

**Salt.** All commentators agree salt symbolises preservation, purity, and covenant fidelity.

Ellicott provides rich cultural background: "From its antiseptic and savoury qualities, salt became the symbol of hospitality, friendship, durability, fidelity. 'To eat bread and salt together' is, in the East, an expression for a league of mutual amity. … When the Arabs make a covenant together, they put salt on the blade of a sword, from whence every one puts a little into his mouth. This constitutes them blood relations" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html. Hence "a covenant of salt" (see Numbers 18:19; 2 Chronicles 13:5) denotes "an indissoluble alliance, an everlasting covenant."

The Pulpit Commentary: "Salt is commanded as symbolizing in things spiritual, because preserving in things physical, incorruption. It is an emblem of an established and enduring covenant" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html.

Enduring Word lists four symbolic dimensions: salt speaks of (1) purity (salt is a stable chemical compound), (2) preservation (it prevents decay), (3) expense (salt was costly), and (4) friendship/relationship (the ancient custom of eating salt together). It also cites Spurgeon: "My brethren, nothing in the service of God is trifling. A pinch of salt may seem to us exceedingly unimportant, but before the Lord it may not be so" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

JFB: "No injunction in the whole law was more sacredly observed than this application of salt" — https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/leviticus/2.htm.

The Reformed devotional from Ligonier notes: "Salt was also a part of the grain offering … most likely because salt is a preservative, and it was the covenant with Yahweh and the people's gratitude for their salvation that sustained Israel" — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/grain-offering.

**"With all your offerings you shall offer salt."** The command extends beyond grain offerings to all sacrifices (cf. Ezekiel 43:24; Mark 9:49). Enduring Word ties this to Jesus' words in Mark 9:49–50 about being "salted with fire" — believers, as living sacrifices, must be seasoned with fire and salt — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

---

### vv. 14–16 — The Grain Offering of Firstfruits

**"Crushed heads of new grain roasted on the fire"** (v. 14). This third form of grain offering used green (fresh) ears of grain, parched/roasted over fire, then beaten out. Ellicott notes this was "a favourite article of food in the East" and cites several Old Testament examples (Leviticus 23:14; Joshua 5:11; 1 Samuel 17:17; Ruth 2:14). The regulations are the same as for the other grain offering forms — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

The Pulpit Commentary observes that Leviticus 2:14–16 should properly follow v. 12 (since v. 13 is a general conclusion about salt for all offerings). "Such transpositions are not uncommon in the Hebrew Scriptures" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/leviticus-2.html.

**Firstfruits theology.** Enduring Word underscores the faith-risk involved: "The first of the harvest and the firstborn of livestock belonged to the LORD. This could be considered risky giving because the land might not yield much more produce, and the cow or ewe might not give birth again — yet the first still belonged to God." Proverbs 3:9–10 is cited as the promise attached to such giving — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

It seems none of the firstfruits grain offering was retained by the priests — all was burned (Enduring Word). The firstfruits grain offering likewise included oil and frankincense (v. 15) and the priest burned the memorial portion "together with all its frankincense" (v. 16).

---

## Where Protestant Traditions Differ

Researching denomination-specific teachers on *this particular chapter* proved difficult; most traditions share a very similar reading of Leviticus 2. The differences are mainly in *emphasis* rather than interpretation:

**Reformed (Ligonier).** Stresses the grain offering as symbolising dedication of *daily labour* to God: "Offering such things symbolized the need to dedicate every aspect of their daily lives to the Creator, including the labor by which they coaxed the grain from the ground." Leaven prohibition is linked to "the decay of sin." Salt represents the sustaining covenant. Emphasis on God's sovereignty over daily provision — https://learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/grain-offering.

**Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word / David Guzik).** Strong typological focus on Christ: "Jesus fulfilled the heart and meaning of the grain offering for us, as the One who perfectly served God, whose service was never touched with leaven in any way." Oil is explicitly the Holy Spirit. The offering prefigures "our service to God." Firstfruits points to Christ's resurrection (1 Corinthians 15:20). The commentary is warmly devotional and application-oriented — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

**Baptist/Evangelical (Constable, from Dallas Theological Seminary).** Emphasises that the grain offering "was acceptable only when offered with the burnt offering. This indicated that one's works were acceptable to God only when they accompanied the offerer's consecration of himself to God." The flour represents "the product of man's labor" — man's works, not his person (the burnt offering). The offerer received *none* of the sacrifice — it all went to God (the memorial) or the priests — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-2.html.

**Anglican (Ellicott, 1878).** More restrained typologically. Practical explanations dominate: oil is "what butter is to ours"; frankincense counteracts the smell of burning flesh; baking vessels are described with archaeological precision. Nevertheless Ellicott identifies salt as a covenant symbol and the memorial as bringing the worshiper into "the grateful remembrance of God" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/leviticus-2.html.

**Spurgeon (Baptist, cited in Enduring Word).** On v. 13, Spurgeon is quoted as saying: "There is a kind of molasses godliness which I can never stomach" (on the command to include salt and exclude honey — sincerity over artificial sweetness). And: "My brethren, nothing in the service of God is trifling. A pinch of salt may seem to us exceedingly unimportant, but before the Lord it may not be so" — https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/leviticus-2/.

---

## Other Views

**Catholic (Haydock, following Challoner and Calmet).** Leaven and honey are excluded to teach exclusion of "all double-dealing and affection to carnal pleasures" from the pure worship of the gospel. Honey was used by Egyptian pagans in sacrifice (citing Herodotus). Unleavened bread reminded the Hebrews of the Exodus. The memorial portion is "to worship and celebrate the name of God" (Louis de Dieu) — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/hcc/leviticus-2.html.

**Modern Scholarship / NET Bible Notes** (cited via Constable): The NET Bible notes that the grain offering "generally accompanied a burnt or peace offering to supplement the meat with bread (the libation provided the drink; cf. Numbers 15:1–10), thus completing the food 'gift' to the LORD. It made atonement … along with the burnt offering (e.g., Leviticus 14:20) or alone as a sin offering for the poor (Leviticus 5:11–13)" — https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/leviticus-2.html. This highlights that the grain offering was part of a *meal* presented to God (animal + grain + wine = complete provision).

**Orthodox** sources (oca.org) did not appear in the search results for this particular chapter.

**Prosperity / Word of Faith / Hyper-Grace** readings of this chapter did not surface in the searches within the approved sites.

---

*Summary note: Leviticus 2 commands a bloodless, voluntary offering of fine flour, oil, frankincense, and salt — without leaven or honey (except in firstfruits, which are not burned on the altar). The memorial portion is burned; the rest feeds the priests. Traditional typology sees the grain offering as picturing Christ's perfect humanity and devoted service (oil = Holy Spirit, no leaven = sinlessness), and the believer's grateful, Spirit-empowered offering of daily work to God.*
